source_findings.detail: Unix launch explicitly sets command.process_group(0) before spawn. The child process ID names its new group; a failed spawn returns infrastructure_error before a ChildGuard exists. Parent runner/shell/supervisor is not deliberately moved into that group.

Cleanup sends SIGKILL to negative known child PID, then kills/waits that child. It does not use kill(0), kill(-1), getpgrp(), pkill or a runner PID. Called on output overflow, 5h worker deadline and after worker exit to terminate pipe-holding descendants. Static evidence supports targeting worker-owned group; failed runner supplied no actual PID/PGID/signal record.

Python subprocess.run invokes the native supervisor argv directly (shell default false), timeout=deadline/1000+120=18120s, no group-wide signal call or new session here. Python timeout kills/waits its direct child. If this fallback kills an unresponsive native supervisor, Rust Drop is not guaranteed and its separately grouped worker could be left alive; that is a residual cleanup limitation, not proof of runner termination or this failure cause.

Earlier capacity prep uses sudo -n timeout --signal=TERM --kill-after=5s 300s for fixed du/rm commands, no --foreground. GNU documented default creates a separate program group. Actual capacity and upload steps completed success at02:24:00/01, before native step; these success records do not supply running native process telemetry. Unresponsive outer capacity supervisor is explicitly unsealed/cleanup-unconfirmed by source.
